title.en: Padmasambhava Tames the Demons of Tibet

region.en: The road of the Guru's march across Tibet (symbolic pin at Samye)
region.zh: 蓮師入藏之路（以桑耶寺為象徵定位）

texts.period: Legendary life of Padmasambhava (Guru Rimpoche), 8th century; Waddell's summary 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. II-IV

summary.en: The Tibetans, beset on every side by malignant devils, warmly welcomed the Guru from Udyana as the bringer of deliverance: arriving in 747 AD he vanquished all the chief devils of the land, sparing most of them on their consenting to become defenders of his religion while he guaranteed that in return they would be duly worshipped and fed. His weapons were the vajra and spells extracted from the Mahayana gospels; his twenty-five disciples each performed a grotesque magical feat - mounting the sunbeams, driving iron bolts into rocks, reviving the slain, making water run upwards, taming wild yaks - and each was instructed in making magic circles for coercing demons and exorcism.
summary.zh: 吐蕃人四面受惡魔擾害，故熱烈歡迎來自鄔仗那的蓮花生大師，視之為解脫者。公元747年入藏後，他降伏境內諸大魔鬼——多數答應充當佛法護衛，大師則保證令其受供養享祭祀。其法器為金剛杵與《摩訶衍那》諸經之咒；二十五位弟子各顯神通：踏日而行、以鐵釘釘入巖石、令死者復生、使水逆流、馴服野犛牛……並各授結界鎮魔之術。

texts.canonical_translation: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism, London 1895 (public domain)

narrative.en:
The founder of Lamaism, Saint Padma-sambhava, 'the Lotus-born one,' usually called by the Tibetans Guru Rimpoche or 'the precious Guru', was a native of Udyana, famed for the proficiency of its priests in sorcery, exorcism and magic: Hiuen Tsiang, writing a century previously, said of Udyana that the people practise the art of using charms and the employment of magical sentences is with them an art and a study. The Tibetans, steeped in superstition which beset them on every side by malignant devils, warmly welcomed the Guru as he brought them deliverance from their terrible tormentors.

Arriving in Tibet in 747 AD at the invitation of King Thi-Sron Detsan, he vanquished all the chief devils of the land, sparing most of them on their consenting to become defenders of his religion, while he on his part guaranteed that in return for such services they would be duly worshipped and fed. Thus, just as the Buddhists in India, in order to secure the support of the semi-aborigines of Bengal, admitted into their system the bloody Durga and other aboriginal demons, so on extending their doctrines throughout Asia they pandered to the popular taste by admitting within the pale of Buddhism the pantheon of those new nations they sought to convert. The Guru's most powerful weapons in warring with the demons were the Vajra (Tibetan, dor-je), symbolic of the thunderbolt of Indra, and spells extracted from the Mahayana gospels, by which he shattered his supernatural adversaries.

Under the zealous patronage of the King he built at Sam-yas in 749 AD the first Tibetan monastery, said to be modelled after the Indian Odantapura of Magadha and entitled the 'Self-sprung immovable shrine', believed to be based on immovable foundations of adamantine laid by the Guru; and there, assisted by the Indian monk Shanta-rakshita - made first abbot - he instituted the order of the Lamas. The leading events of his march through Tibet and his subjugation of the local devils indicate the original habitats of several of the pre-Lamaist demons; each of the demons of the indigenous Bon-pa religion was assigned its proper place in the Lamaist pantheon, and primitive Lamaism may be defined as a priestly mixture of Sivaite mysticism, magic and Indo-Tibetan demonolatry overlaid by a thin varnish of Mahayana Buddhism.

Padma-sambhava had twenty-five disciples, each credited with magical power, mostly of a grotesque character: Nam-k'a s'in-po mounted the sunbeams; San-gye-ye-se drove iron bolts into rocks; Gyal-wa-ch'og-yan changed his head into a horse's and neighed thrice; K'ar-ch'en Ch'o-gyal revived the slain; Pal-ki-ye-se overcame three fiendesses; Pal-ki-Sen-ge enslaved demons, nymphs and genii; Vairocana obtained the five heavenly eyes of knowledge; Dorje-Dun Jem travelled invisibly as the wind; Ye-se-Nan visited the fairy world; Shu-bu-pal-sen made water run upwards; Gyal-wai-Lodoi raised ghosts and converted the corpse into gold; Ten-pai-nam-k'a tamed wild yaks of the northern desert; 'Odan-Wan-p'yug dived into water like a fish; Ma-t'og rin-ch'en crushed adamant to powder and ate it like meal; Pal-kyi Dor-je passed through rocks and mountains; and Lan-dod Kon-ch'og wielded and repelled thunderbolts. And these disciples he instructed in the way of making magic circles for coercing the demons and for exorcism.

The Guru's departure from Tibet was as miraculous in character as his life: addressing the king he said that in Jambudvip were five Raksha countries crowded with men-eating devils who, if not conquered, would depopulate the whole world of Jambudvip, and except me none other can subdue them - thither must I now go. Accompanied by the king and nobles and his two fairy wives, he went to the Gung-thang La on the northern confines of Tibet, and there, after giving farewell advice to keep the doctrine and the revelations hidden in caves throughout the land, he was enveloped in a glorious rainbow-halo within which appeared the four great heroes of the world, who assisted him in mounting the celestial horse-car named Ialaha, in which he was borne away through the sky in a south-westerly direction amid heavenly music and showers of flowers. The assembled multitude remained transfixed as if dead, and after twenty-five days and nights could still see the Guru's celestial party, like a shooting star, sailing away through the sky till lost to sight. He reached Singala after about two days' journey, penetrating the iron palace, entered the body of the Raksha king named 'He of the Skull rosary', and preached the doctrine to the thousand daughters of the Raksha; at the capital Sando-pal-ri, abstracting the life of the demon-king Yaksha Me-wal and entering his body, the Guru reigns there supreme over the Rakshas even up till the present day, and in perpetual youth is preaching there the doctrine of Lamaism in a paradise which rivals that of Amitabha's western heaven of Sukhavati. And notwithstanding his grotesque charlatanism and uncelibate life, he is deified and worshipped as the 'second Buddha', his image under 'The eight worshipful Forms' found in every Tibetan temple of the old sect.
narrative.notes: Cultural function: the demon-taming legend is the charter of the Nyingma order and of the whole Tantric apparatus of Tibetan religion - every protective deity and every exorcistic rite traces itself to the Guru's bargain with the local gods, and the landscape of Tibet is mapped as the sequence of his subjugations.

functions: Charter of the Nyingma (Old School): the local demons of the Bon are converted into 'defenders of the faith' under contract of worship
Explains the Tibetan religious landscape: each demon's original habitat is remembered as a stage of the Guru's march
Authorizes exorcistic rites: the twenty-five disciples' feats and the magic circles are the pedigree of the sorcerer's craft
Establishes the terma doctrine - the revelations hidden in caves throughout the land, to be 'discovered' by later saints

variants.name: The legendary life of the Guru
variants.text_tradition: Padma bka'-thang and later Nyingma hagiographies
variants.summary: The full hagiographies add the princess Mandarava, a sister of Shanta-rakshita, whom the Guru married, and the birth-legend from a lotus; Waddell's summary here follows the standard compiled tradition.

variants.name: The historical view
variants.text_tradition: Rockhill's Life of the Buddha, ch. VII
variants.summary: Rockhill's sober account has Shantarakshita advising the king to invite Padma Sambhava of Udyana after his own teachings met opposition; the demon-taming belongs to the later legendary accretion.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Padmasambhava is a living devotional centre of Tibetan Buddhism; passages below are paraphrases of the 1895 public-domain summary, not verbatim liturgy, and the tradition is treated respectfully.

title.en: Vairocana Banished and the Red Rahula She-Devil
title.zh: 毗盧遮那流放與「紅羅睺羅魔女」

region.en: Eastern province of Kham (symbolic pin at Chamdo)
region.zh: 藏東康區（以昌都為象徵定位）

texts.period: Reign of Thi-Sron Detsan (8th century); Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. II

summary.en: The most learned of the young Lamas, Vairocana, translated many Sanskrit works into Tibetan, but his usefulness was interrupted by the Tibetan wife of Thi-Sron Detsan, who, in bitter opposition to the King's reforms and instigated by the Bon-pa priests, secured the banishment of Vairocana to the eastern province of Kham by a scheme similar to that practised by Potiphar's wife. But, on her being forthwith afflicted with leprosy, she relented, and the young Bairo-tsana was recalled and effected her cure - she is still handed down to history as the 'Red Rahula she-devil', while Vairocana is made an incarnation of Buddha's faithful attendant and cousin Ananda.
summary.zh: 青年僧中最博學的毗盧遮那譯經甚多，卻遭赤松德贊的藏籍王妃阻撓——她受苯教僧唆使、堅決反對王的改革，以「波提法之妻」之計將毗盧遮那貶至東部康區。然王妃隨即染癩，悔悟之下迎回毗盧遮那，並由他醫癒其疾——她從此被史書稱為「紅羅睺羅魔女」，而毗盧遮那則被奉為佛陀近侍阿難之化身。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The most learned of these young Lamas was Vairocana, who translated many Sanskrit works into Tibetan, though his usefulness was interrupted for a while by the Tibetan wife of Thi-Sron Detsan; who in her bitter opposition to the King's reforms, and instigated by the Bon-pa priests, secured the banishment of Vairocana to the eastern province of Kham by a scheme similar to that practised by Potiphar's wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: But, on her being forthwith afflicted with leprosy, she relented, and the young Bairo-tsana was recalled and effected her cure; she is still, however, handed down to history as the Red Rahula she-devil, while Vairocana is made an incarnation of Buddha's faithful attendant and cousin Ananda - and on account of his having translated many orthodox scriptures, he is credited with the composition and hiding away of many of the fictitious scriptures of the unreformed Lamas, which were afterwards discovered as revelations.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: The Black-Hat Devil-Dancer Who Shot the King

region.en: Below the king's palace at Lhasa (symbolic pin at the Jokhang, Lhasa)
region.zh: 拉薩王宮之下（以大昭寺為象徵定位）

texts.period: Assassination of Ralpachen's successor-era king, c. 899-925 AD; Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. II

summary.en: Ralpachen's devotion to Buddhism led to his murder at the instigation of his younger brother Lan Darma - the so-called Julian of Lamaism - who then persecuted the Lamas, desecrated the temples, burned many of their books and forced many to become butchers. But the persecution was short-lived: Lan Darma was assassinated in the third year of his reign by a Lama of Lha-lung named Pal-dorje, who to effect his purpose assumed the guise of a strolling black-hat devil-dancer and hid in his ample sleeves a bow and arrow; his dancing below the king's palace attracted the king, who summoned the dancer to his presence - where the disguised Lama shot him with the arrow, which proved almost immediately fatal. In the resulting tumult the Lama sped away on a black horse tethered near at hand, and riding on plunged through the Kyi river on the outskirts of Lhasa, whence his horse emerged in its natural white colour, as it had been merely blackened by soot - and this murderous incident forms a part of the modern Lamaist masquerade.
summary.zh: 赤祖德贊因崇佛而遇弒，其弟朗達瑪繼位——人稱「藏傳之朱利安」——毀廟焚經，強僧操刀為屠。然迫害未及三年：拉龍貝吉多傑扮作遊方黑帽咒舞者，袖藏弓箭，於王宮下起舞；王召見之，趁机放箭，王中箭立斃。亂中貝吉多傑騎近旁之黑馬疾馳，渡拉薩河——馬出水面竟復原為白色，蓋其黑乃煙熏所致——此刺殺之舞至今仍是藏歷新年跳神之程式。

sensitivity.note: Historical-legendary material; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: Lan Darma ascended the throne after Ralpachen's murder and at once commenced to persecute the Lamas and did his utmost to uproot the religion; he desecrated the temples and several monasteries, burned many of their books, and treated the Lamas with the grossest indignity, forcing many to become butchers. But Lan Darma's persecution was very mild for a religious one, and very short-lived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was assassinated in the third year of his reign by a Lama of Lha-luh named Pal-dorje, who has since been canonized by his grateful church, and this murderous incident forms a part of the modern Lamaist masquerade. This Lama, to effect his purpose, assumed the guise of a strolling black-hat devil-dancer, and hid in his ample sleeves a bow and arrow; his dancing below the king's palace attracted the attention of the king, who summoned the dancer to his presence - where the disguised Lama seized an opportunity while near the king to shoot him with the arrow, which proved almost immediately fatal. In the resulting tumult the Lama sped away on a black horse tethered near at hand, and riding on, plunged through the Kyi river on the outskirts of Lhasa, whence his horse emerged in its natural white colour, as it had been merely blackened by soot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Pehar in the Box: The State Oracle of Nechung
title.zh: 寶盒中的白哈爾：乃瓊護法

region.en: Nechung temple, near Drepung, west of Lhasa (symbolic pin at Nechung)
region.zh: 哲蚌寺附近的乃瓊寺（以乃瓊寺為象徵定位）

texts.period: Nechung oracle tradition (mediaeval to 19th century); Waddell 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Sorcery and Necromancy

summary.en: The demon-king Pehar, originally a god of the Turki tribes named 'The White Overcast Sky', was brought to Tibet by Padmasambhava and made religious guardian of the first monastery, Sam-ya. Centuries later his spirit transferred itself to Ts'al-gun-t'an and said to a Lama named Z'ari, 'Let us go to Udyana' - whereupon the Lama shut up the possessed man in a box and flung it into the river Kyi; the abbot of Depung, who had prophesied the previous day that a box would float down the river, had his pupils seize it, and when they opened it a great fire came out and disappeared into a tree, and a dead man's body was found within. By the abbot's prayers the spirit consented to return to the body, and the resuscitated corpse, refusing to enter the pure monastery of Depung on the plea of being uncelibate, requested to be granted 'a small dwelling' where he stood - hence the name of the place Na-ch'un, 'the small dwelling'; and the identical tree is still to be seen there.
summary.zh: 護法神白哈爾本為突厥部落之神「陰天白」，由蓮花生攜入吐蕃，任桑耶寺首座護法。數百年後其神識遷至拉薩近郊，向喇嘛扎日言「我們去鄔仗那吧！」——喇嘛遂將被附身者鎖入木箱，拋入吉曲河。哲蚌寺住持前日已預言「河上將漂來一箱」，弟子們截住之；開箱時火焰騰起沒入一株樹中，箱內只餘一具死屍。經住持祈請，神魂重返屍身；復活者自言不守淨戒、不肯入哲蚌大寺，只求在立足處賜「一小居」——乃瓊（意為「小居」）之名由此而來，那株樹至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Living oracle tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: This demon-king was originally a god of the Turki tribes, and named The White Overcast Sky, and on account of his Turki descent the popular epic of the famous prince Kesar, who had conquered the Turki tribes, is not permitted to be recited at Depung, under whose aegis the Na-ch'un oracle resides, for fear of offending the latter. He was brought to Tibet by Padma-sambhava in Thi-Sron Detsan's reign, and made the Ch'o-Kyon or religious guardian of the first monastery, Sam-ya.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: The legend states that the spirit of Pehar entered into a resident of Ts'al-gun-t'an, and said to a Lama named Z'ari, Let us go to Udyana; the Lama then shut up the possessed man in a box, which he flung into the river Kyi. Now the abbot of De-pung had prophesied the previous day to his pupils, saying, a box will float down the river, go find it and seize it; the pupils found the box and brought it to the spot where the Na-ch'un temple now stands, and there they opened it, and lo! a great fire came out and disappeared into a tree, and the dead body of a man was found in the box; but by the prayers of the abbot the spirit consented to return to the body. And the resuscitated corpse, refusing to enter the pure monastery of De-pung on the plea of being uncelibate, requested to be granted a small dwelling where he stood - hence the name of the place Na-ch'un, the small dwelling; and the identical tree is still to be seen there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

title.zh: 政府御用占卜師乃瓊神巫

region.en: Nechung temple and the Jo-wo temple at Lhasa (symbolic pin at Lhasa)
region.zh: 乃瓊寺與拉薩大昭寺（以拉薩為象徵定位）

texts.period: State-oracle tradition, organized by the fifth Grand Lama (17th century); Waddell's observations 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on Sorcery and Necromancy

summary.en: The chief wizards are called Defenders of the Faith, and the highest of these, Na-ch'un, is the government oracle, consulted on all important state occasions; he was made a Lama of the yellow sect and state-oracle by the fifth Grand Lama, the reason alleged being that he frustrated an attempt of the Newar merchants of Lhasa to poison the tea-cistern at the great festival by driving a knife through the vessel. Once a year he proceeds in great pomp to Lhasa, is accommodated in a special temple close to the east of the great Jo-wo temple, and prophesies the events of the year; the applicant's request must be presented in writing, and when a sufficient number have accumulated the augur is disclosed in a wildly ecstatic state - he throws rice at the applicants, and becoming more inflamed by fury, falls down in convulsions and then replies to questions, the replies noted by attendant scribes and sealed by the sorcerer himself on his recovery.
summary.zh: 眾巫之首稱「護法」，其極者乃瓊，即政府占卜之神諭，凡國家大事皆諮之。五世達賴將其納入黃教僧籍、立為國師神巫——相傳因其挫敗拉薩尼泊爾商人在大法會中下毒茶池之謀（一劍刺穿茶缸）。歲首次日，神巫儀仗入拉薩，宿於大昭寺東之專廟，預言一年之事；求示者須以書面呈請，積至相當數量，神巫狂迷而出——向請示者擲米，愈舞愈狂，癲倒抽搐，方才作答；回答由侍立書記記錄，事後由神巫蘇醒時親自鈐印。

sensitivity.note: Living oracle tradition; paraphrase of public-domain translation.

passages.text: The chief wizards are called Defenders of the Faith, and the highest of these, namely Na-ch'un, is the government oracle, and is consulted on all important state occasions and undertakings. The chief of these necromancers was first brought into the order of the Lamas by the fifth Grand Lama, who seems to have felt, like the Roman governors, the necessity for placing the divination for government service under the control of the priests, and he admitted the augur of Na-ch'un to the brotherhood and made him the state-oracle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

passages.text: This state-sorcerer proceeds in great pomp to Lhasa once a year, attended by the magistrate of De-pung, and is accommodated in a special temple close to the east of the great Jo-wo temple, where he prophesies the events of the year. The applicant to the oracle must have his request presented in writing, and when a sufficient number of applications have accumulated, the augur is disclosed in a wildly ecstatic state; he throws rice at the applicants, and becoming more inflamed by fury, he falls down in convulsions and then replies to questions addressed to him. The replies are noted down by attendant scribes, and the document is afterwards sealed - it is said by the sorcerer himself on his recovery - and the utterances are often couched in poetry or allegory, with the brevity and ambiguousness of an oracular response.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.

title.en: Gesar Among the Suitors of the Chinese Princess
title.zh: 求娶文成公主的格薩爾王

region.en: The epic world of Ling, northeastern Tibet (symbolic pin in Kham)
region.zh: 嶺國史詩世界——康區（以康區為象徵定位）

texts.period: Gesar epic (oral, earliest written recensions mediaeval); Waddell's notice 1895

source.work: L. A. Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet or Lamaism (1895), ch. on The Scriptures and Literature

summary.en: The best-known of Tibetan tales is that of Ge-sar - 'Czar or Caesar' - described as a mighty war-like king of northern Asia, who is made to figure as a suitor for the hand of the Chinese princess before her marriage with Sron Tsan Gampo, although it is evident the legendary accounts of him must be more ancient; the epic is so identified with the Turki enemies of the oracle-god Pehar that its recitation is forbidden at Depung, under whose aegis the Na-ch'un oracle resides, for fear of offending the latter.
summary.zh: 藏地最著名的故事是格薩爾——「愷撒」之音——被描寫為北亞驍勇之王，甚至被編入文成公主求婚者的行列（其傳說實遠早於此）。因格薩爾征服突厥部落，而突厥正乃護法白哈爾之敵，故哲蚌寺——乃瓊神諭所寄之寺——禁誦此史詩，以免觸怒護法。

sensitivity.note: Living epic tradition (still recited across the Tibetan culture area); paraphrase of public-domain notice.

passages.text: The best known of these tales is that of Ge-sar, who is described as a mighty war-like king of northern Asia, and who is made to figure as a suitor for the hand of the Chinese princess before her marriage with Sron Tsan Gam-po, although it is evident the legendary accounts of him must be more ancient. And on account of his Turki descent the popular epic of the famous prince Kesar, who had conquered the Turki tribes, is not permitted to be recited at De-pung, under whose aegis the Na-ch'un oracle resides, for fear of offending the latter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Waddell, The Buddhism of Tibet (1895); not verbatim.
